title: Rabin–Karp Rolling Hash
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Rabin–Karp slides a fixed-length window by removing the leading character's contribution and appending the new one, updating the hash in O(1) per shift.
short: Update the window hash instead of recomputing it.
long: Update the window hash instead of recomputing it. With verification of candidate matches the expected running time is O(n+m); a worst-case collision-rich input can be slower.
proof: Treating the window as a base-b polynomial, removal and appending are O(1) modular operations.
consequence: Rolling hashes enable multi-pattern search and plagiarism detection.

title: Rabin–Karp Expected versus Worst Case
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Rabin–Karp has expected O(n+m) time under random hashing but O(nm) worst case if an adversary forces hash collisions at every alignment.
short: Verification fixes correctness, not the collision count.
long: Verification fixes correctness, not the collision count. Using a large random prime makes adversarial collisions unlikely.
proof: Each of n alignments can in the worst case produce a collision requiring an O(m) string comparison.
consequence: It is a Monte Carlo style speed-up unless collisions are fully eliminated.

title: Hash Collisions Are Inevitable
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Any hash function mapping the infinite set of strings into finitely many hash values must collide on two different strings.
short: Pigeonhole principle forbids collision-free hashing.
long: Pigeonhole principle forbids collision-free hashing. Therefore every hash-based string algorithm needs either verification or an explicit collision probability bound.
proof: There are infinitely many strings and only 2^k possible k-bit hash values, so some value has multiple preimages.
consequence: Hash-based searches trade a small collision risk for speed.

title: Boyer–Moore Bad Character Rule
subject: String Algorithms
statement: On a mismatch the bad-character rule slides the pattern so that the mismatching text character aligns with its last occurrence in the pattern.
short: Jump past text characters the pattern cannot match.
long: Jump past text characters the pattern cannot match. Used alone it can still degrade to O(nm) on repetitive text.
proof: Any alignment placing a different pattern character opposite c cannot match, so those alignments are skipped safely.
consequence: It gives large average-case jumps for long patterns and large alphabets.

title: Boyer–Moore Good Suffix Rule
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The good-suffix rule shifts a pattern after a mismatch so that the matched suffix realigns with its next occurrence or with a matching prefix.
short: Use the matched tail to choose a safe jump.
long: Use the matched tail to choose a safe jump. Combined with the bad-character rule it is the classic Boyer–Moore algorithm; Galil's rule restores O(n+m) worst case.
proof: Any smaller shift would place a pattern substring inconsistent with the characters already matched.
consequence: Good-suffix preprocessing makes Boyer–Moore very fast in practice.

title: Boyer–Moore Sublinear Comparisons
subject: String Algorithms
statement: On long patterns and realistic text, Boyer–Moore can inspect only O(n/m) character alignments, far fewer than the text length.
short: Scan right to left and skip large blocks.
long: Scan right to left and skip large blocks. This is a best-case or average statement; worst-case safeguards require Galil's rule.
proof: Right-to-left matching usually fails early, and each failure shifts the pattern by close to its full length.
consequence: It is a classic example of an algorithm whose practical behaviour beats its naive worst-case picture.

title: Horspool Simplified Bad-Character Search
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Horspool's algorithm compares right to left but always shifts by the last-character bad-character table, avoiding good-suffix preprocessing.
short: One shift table is often enough in practice.
long: One shift table is often enough in practice. It is a simplification of Boyer–Moore with competitive real-world speed.
proof: The shift table computed from the pattern's last character gives a safe alignment after each mismatch.
consequence: It is a popular lightweight substring-search routine.

title: Aho–Corasick Multiple-Pattern Automaton
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Aho–Corasick builds a trie of patterns augmented with failure links, finding all occurrences of all patterns in a text in one pass.
short: A trie with failure links is a finite-state matcher.
long: A trie with failure links is a finite-state matcher. m is the total length of all patterns.
proof: Failure links lead to the longest proper suffix that is a trie prefix, so each text character advances the state at most once amortised.
consequence: It is the standard solution for keyword filtering and intrusion detection.

title: Aho–Corasick Output Links
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Propagating output links through failure chains reports every pattern ending at a state in time proportional to the number of reports.
short: Inherit matches from suffix states.
long: Inherit matches from suffix states. Without output links, reporting all matches could cost time proportional to the number of patterns per text position.
proof: A pattern ending at a suffix of the current string is stored along the failure chain, so each report is traversed once.
consequence: It makes multi-pattern matching output-sensitive.

title: Suffix Tree Compresses All Suffixes
subject: String Algorithms
statement: A suffix tree is a compressed trie of all suffixes of a string, using O(n) nodes and supporting substring searches in O(m) time.
short: Every substring is a prefix of some suffix.
long: Every substring is a prefix of some suffix. Edges are labelled by substrings, and compressed paths eliminate unary nodes.
proof: A compressed trie of n suffixes has at most 2n nodes because leaves number n and internal nodes have at least two children.
consequence: Suffix trees answer many string queries in linear or near-linear time.

title: Suffix Array Definition
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The suffix array of a string lists the starting positions of all suffixes in lexicographic order.
short: A sorted list of suffixes replaces a tree.
long: A sorted list of suffixes replaces a tree. It uses O(n) space and, with an LCP array, supports many suffix-tree-like queries.
proof: Sorting suffixes is equivalent to sorting all substrings that extend to the end of the string.
consequence: Suffix arrays are simpler and more compact than suffix trees in practice.

title: Suffix Array Doubling Construction
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Doubling sorts suffixes by their first 2^k characters using rank pairs and counting sort, constructing the suffix array in O(n log n) time.
short: Sort by length-2 substrings, then double repeatedly.
long: Sort by length-2 substrings, then double repeatedly. SA-IS improves this to O(n) time for constant alphabets.
proof: The ranks for length 2^k determine the ranks for length 2^{k+1} via lexicographic order of rank pairs.
consequence: It is the standard implementable suffix-array construction.

title: Suffix Tree from Suffix Array and LCP
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The LCP array of adjacent suffixes together with the suffix array determines the suffix-tree topology.
short: LCP values give internal-node depths.
long: LCP values give internal-node depths. A stack-based scan of the LCP array builds the tree in linear time.
proof: Adjacent suffixes in suffix-array order share deepest prefixes given by LCP values, matching tree internal nodes.
consequence: It lets implementations enjoy suffix-array compactness and suffix-tree power.

title: Ukkonen's Online Suffix Tree
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Ukkonen's algorithm builds a suffix tree left to right in O(n) time for constant alphabets.
short: Extend all suffixes incrementally with suffix links.
long: Extend all suffixes incrementally with suffix links. It is online: each prefix's tree is valid before reading the next character.
proof: An active point tracks the current insertion position and suffix links jump between related nodes, bounding total work.
consequence: It is the classic linear-time suffix-tree construction.

title: Kasai's LCP Array Algorithm
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Scanning suffixes in text order while carrying the current match length computes the LCP array in O(n) time.
short: Adjacent suffixes in text order can reuse the previous comparison length.
long: Adjacent suffixes in text order can reuse the previous comparison length. Decrementing the carried value by one per position keeps total comparisons linear.
proof: If suffixes at i-1 and j share l characters, suffixes at i and j+1 share at least l-1.
consequence: It turns an O(n log n) or quadratic LCP computation into linear time.

title: LCP Array and Longest Repeated Substring
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The maximum entry of the LCP array is the length of the longest substring appearing at least twice in the string.
short: Adjacent suffixes in sorted order share the longest repeats.
long: Adjacent suffixes in sorted order share the longest repeats. Any repeated substring appears as a prefix of two suffixes whose LCP is at least its length.
proof: The two suffixes with a common repeated prefix occupy positions in the suffix array with all intervening LCP values at least that length, so the maximum captures it.
consequence: It gives a linear-time longest-repeat query after suffix-array construction.

title: Burrows–Wheeler Transform
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The BWT sorts all rotations of a string and writes the last column of the resulting matrix, often grouping repeated characters into long runs.
short: Reorder characters to improve compressibility.
long: Reorder characters to improve compressibility. It is invertible when the original string ends with a unique sentinel character.
proof: Sorting rotations creates rows whose last characters correspond to preceding characters in the original text.
consequence: It underpins bzip2 and modern genomic compressors.

title: BWT Invertibility via LF Mapping
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The k-th occurrence of a character in the last BWT column corresponds to the k-th occurrence in the first column, allowing the original string to be reconstructed.
short: Occurrence ranks link last and first columns.
long: Occurrence ranks link last and first columns. Repeated LF steps trace the text backwards from the sentinel.
proof: Sorting rotations preserves the relative order of equal-character rows, so occurrence ranks match across columns.
consequence: LF mapping enables both inversion and suffix-array-free text searches.

title: FM-Index Substring Search
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The FM-index searches a pattern backwards in the BWT by maintaining a suffix-array interval and updating it with rank queries.
short: Extend matches one character at a time using BWT ranks.
long: Extend matches one character at a time using BWT ranks. It provides compressed full-text search with space close to the compressed text.
proof: The interval of suffixes prefixed by cP is obtained from the interval for P by applying LF mapping restricted to c.
consequence: It is foundational for genomic short-read alignment.

title: Suffix Automaton States
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The suffix automaton of a string is a minimal DFA accepting all its substrings, with at most 2n-1 states for a string of length n.
short: A compact automaton for every substring.
long: A compact automaton for every substring. It can be built online in O(n) time for constant alphabets.
proof: Each extension creates at most one new state, and cloning splits at most one existing state.
consequence: It supports substring counting and longest-common-substring queries efficiently.

title: Levenshtein Edit Distance DP
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Edit distance with insertions, deletions and substitutions of cost 1 is computed by DP in O(nm) time and O(min(n,m)) space.
short: Fill a grid of prefix-to-prefix costs.
long: Fill a grid of prefix-to-prefix costs. If characters match, the diagonal value is inherited at no cost.
proof: The last operation in an optimal alignment must be one of the three edits handled by the recurrence.
consequence: It is the standard measure for spell-checking and sequence comparison.

title: Damerau–Levenshtein Transpositions
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Damerau–Levenshtein distance additionally allows swapping two adjacent characters as a single edit.
short: Adjacent typos cost one edit, not two.
long: Adjacent typos cost one edit, not two. The optimal string alignment variant forbids overlapping transpositions and is computed by the simple four-case recurrence.
proof: Adding a transposition case to the standard edit-distance recurrence handles swapped adjacent characters.
consequence: It improves spell-checking accuracy for common keyboard errors.

title: Hirschberg Linear-Space LCS
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Hirschberg's algorithm computes an actual longest common subsequence in O(nm) time and O(min(n,m)) space by divide and conquer over rows.
short: Recompute forward and backward DP at the split row.
long: Recompute forward and backward DP at the split row. It retains the standard LCS time bound while eliminating the quadratic table.
proof: A middle row from forward and backward passes identifies the optimal split point, after which the two halves are solved recursively.
consequence: It makes LCS feasible for long sequences with limited memory.

title: Manacher's Linear Palindrome Search
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Manacher's algorithm finds the longest palindromic substring centred at every position in O(n) time by reusing mirrored radii.
short: Palindrome radii inside a known palindrome mirror each other.
long: Palindrome radii inside a known palindrome mirror each other. Separator characters unify even- and odd-length palindromes.
proof: Each centre's radius expands only beyond the current rightmost palindrome boundary, so total expansions are linear.
consequence: It is the optimal algorithm for longest-palindrome queries.

title: Rope Balanced Tree for Strings
subject: String Algorithms
statement: A rope represents a string as a balanced binary tree whose leaves hold short substrings, supporting concatenation and splitting in O(log n) time.
short: Avoid copying long strings when editing.
long: Avoid copying long strings when editing. Profitable weight balancing keeps tree height logarithmic after updates.
proof: Concatenation creates a new root; splitting follows one path and rebalances the two resulting trees.
consequence: Ropes are used in text editors and persistent string libraries.
